questions.question: If a program always trivially does what it does, doesn't calling something a 'bug' just depend on which specification you happen to pick?

passages.quote: the program itself provides a specification for what it will do. And with respect to this specification the program will always just “do what it does”, with no possibility of “having a bug”.
In other words, it seems as if, whatever constraint we give, there’ll somehow always be machines that will insidiously escape it—in effect “having an insidious bug”.

questions.question: If visual simplicity guarantees no bugs and complexity only raises suspicion, how confident can we be about cases whose fluctuations just look 'random' but bounded?

passages.quote: But there’s no obvious way to be sure—and to guarantee that nothing crazy will ever happen—that would lead to a bug.

But there are still cases where—despite that complexity—the feature of behavior that we are concerned about (here, the successful doubling of any input) still always reliably happens, without any bugs.

questions.question: The doubling cellular automaton's complicated pattern was shown bug-free by a structural argument—so why can't every irreducible system get a similar finite proof?

passages.quote: So, yes, even though the patterns in this case look complicated, they must always eventually stabilize—and the underlying cellular automaton must always correctly “double its input”, with no bugs.
But if there’s computational irreducibility one would in effect need an infinite number of facts to do that.

questions.question: When a proof search for a buggy Turing machine never succeeds, how do we know that's because no proof exists rather than we just haven't looked long enough?

passages.quote: But now—however far we go—we never find a proof

because, in fact, the result we’re trying to prove isn’t true, so there isn’t a proof. And we know that because, if we test sufficiently many cases of the Turing machine, we can explicitly find the bug.

questions.question: If computational irreducibility means a system's behavior can't be predicted without running it, how can any proof ever guarantee a program has no bugs?

passages.quote: One important feature of computational irreducibility is that whenever it’s present, there must also be pockets of computational reducibility present.

questions.question: If random testing can't systematically dodge a program's rare 'special corner' bugs, why might it still fail to catch them even after huge numbers of trials?

passages.quote: Of course, even if the sampling doesn’t “systematically avoid” bugs, it might just not hit them, because the bugs exist only in some “special corner” of possible inputs.
Still, the number of samples might just not be large enough to ever hit a bug—given the density of bugs that are present.

questions.question: Doesn't fully understanding why a program can never have bugs mean it wasn't worth actually running as a program in the first place?

passages.quote: if you can really understand everything your program can do that basically means the program is doing something computationally reducible, and you probably in the end didn’t actually need to run the program with all its steps to get the result you wanted.

any time you write a program that actually needs to be written (in the sense that it’s achieving at least some irreducible computation), it’ll have the possibility of doing something you didn’t expect or foresee—and that you might consider a bug.

questions.question: If a well-designed language packs computational irreducibility into its primitives, does that remove the risk of bugs or just relocate where they can occur?

passages.quote: In effect, what’s happened is that most of the computational irreducibility has been packed into the primitives of the language, so that what’s left over is the part that’s accessible to us humans, and that maps into our natural patterns of thinking.

any time you write a program that actually needs to be written (in the sense that it’s achieving at least some irreducible computation), it’ll have the possibility of doing something you didn’t expect or foresee—and that you might consider a bug.
